summary: A status report on an experiment in letting users on different ARPANET hosts talk to each other from their terminals, ask who is online, and perhaps share programs. It grows out of a 1971 Network Working Group discussion of inter-entity communication. The RFC describes the experiment, not a finished protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Kids in different classrooms wanting a way to see who else is around and chat with them. This note tests such a way for computers.

questions: how did early arpanet users chat
subtitle: An experiment in letting network users find and communicate with each other across systems.

tldr.problem: Users on different ARPANET systems wanted to find out who else was online, communicate with other users, and allow remote debugging assistance across system boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: Inter-Entity Communication (IEC) provides commands like WHO, WHERE, and LINK to allow users to discover who is available on remote systems and establish connections for conversation. Implementations exist at MIT and BBN using different interface designs but compatible protocols.
tldr.outcome: An operational experiment that demonstrates network-wide user interaction and lays groundwork for future conferencing and collaborative features.

today: IEC is a historical precursor to modern chat and collaboration systems. While the specific protocol is obsolete, the core ideas of network-wide user presence, discovery, and real-time communication remain central to today's workplace communication platforms.

sections.title: Inter-Entity Communication
sections.content:
RFC 441 reports on an experiment called Inter-Entity Communication (IEC) that enables users on different ARPANET systems to find and communicate with each other. The inspiration came from capabilities already common within individual time-sharing systems: commands like WHO (list current users), TALK (chat with another user), and LINK (connect terminals). IEC extends these capabilities across host boundaries.

The experiment emerged from discussions at the October 1971 Network Working Group meeting at MIT. Implementations are now available at MIT-DMCG and at BBN on TENEX systems, with a protocol that attempts to be compatible across different computer architectures.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers on the network wanted a way to let their users find each other and chat, similar to what single computers already allowed.

sections.title: Ports and Connections
sections.content:
IEC introduces the concept of ports to manage multiple communication streams. A user's terminal can have input and output ports connected to different entities: other consultants, running jobs, or remote systems. Users can open or close ports selectively, for example allowing a consultant to control a job while preventing terminal input, or opening ports for conference-style multi-user communication.

The RFC includes a diagram showing a user terminal with a job and two remote consultants, each connected through separate ports that can be opened or closed independently. This flexibility enables both point-to-point communication and more complex scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like having different phone lines: you can connect each line to a different person and switch between them.

sections.title: Using IEC
sections.content:
The user interfaces differ between implementations. On MIT-DMCG systems, commands include WHO (list users on a host), WHERE (find a user across all known servers), OPEN and CLOSE (manage ports), CONNECT (establish a connection to another user), and PORT MAP (visualize all ports). On TENEX systems, the RSEXEC subsystem provides similar capabilities through an extended command shell that works across network boundaries.

The RFC includes detailed protocol specifications using 36-bit words, various encoding formats, and message types. Socket 245 is assigned for this service. The authors invite further experimentation and are developing improved protocols while noting this interim version is already operational.
sections.plainLanguage: You type commands like WHERE ALICE to find Alice, then CONNECT ALICE to send her a message.
